newsitem.title: UK: UK's Williams, Chubb plan lock-up.
newsitem.headline: UK's Williams, Chubb plan lock-up.

text.p: Britain's Williams Holdings Plc on Friday launched a recommended 1.3 billion pound ($2.12 billion) offer for Chubb Security Plc in a lock-up that would create a world force in security and fire protection.
The deal would unite major brand names in the security industry -- including Yale, Kidd and Chubb -- and create a company with combined annual sales of some 2.7 billion pounds.
"From an industrial point of view, it is an absolutely logical fit," Williams chief executive Roger Carr told Reuters in an interview.
Williams said its Yale and Kidde businesses were particularly strong in the Americas and continental Europe and also had a growing presence in the Far East.
Chubb, in comparison, had limited business in the Americas but considerable strength in Britain, and a large presence in the Asia-Pacific region, the company said.
Williams said it expected to receive regulatory clearance for the deal and overcome any possible monopoly concerns.

"We clearly have issues in that area where there is an overlap, but we are confident that we have solutions to those issues and we're comfortable that we'll achieve a fair and totally acceptable settlement," Carr said.
He added that he did not expect the deal to be referred to Britain's Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
Williams' offer, which valued Chubb at 450 pence per share based on Thursday's closing share prices, is composed of about 50 percent stock and 50 percent cash.
The company is offering two new Williams shares and 704.12 pence in cash for every three Chubb shares.

Williams said its offer represented a 37 percent premium over the closing price of 329.5p for Chubb shares on February 11 before takeover speculation sparked a surge in Chubb shares, which is being investigated by the London Stock Exchange.
Chubb's shares rose five pence to 425 by 1135 GMT, while Williams' shares fell 35-1/2 pence to 301-1/2.

Chubb's rise followed sharp gains on Thursday, when its stock soared 82 pence, or more than 24 percent, to a new year high of 423 pence as the company said it was in talks that might lead to an offer for the group.
Carr said the deal, which will be partly financed with a 1.0 billion pound credit facility, would be modestly dilutive in the first 12 months and earnings enhancing thereafter.
Williams forecast an 11 percent rise in 1996 pre-tax pre-exceptional profits to 243 million pounds.
It expected to pay a final dividend of 9.25 pence net, making 15.05 pence for the full year.
Carr noted that Chubb had been one of the attractions behind Williams' failed bid for Racal Electronics Plc, then Chubb's parent, in 1991.
"(Chubb's subsequent demerger) was a response to our bid, but in many ways it created a separate company which became a perfect fit for us later on," he said.
Williams, which also has home improvement operations, did not plan to make further disposals following its recent 360 million pound sale of 15 home products businesses.
"We've got a balanced business -- we'll have a billion pounds (in sales) in fire, a billion in security and 630 to 640 million in home improvements. And that's a very healthy balance," he said.
